newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Yawns, derision greet new S.Korean labour law.
newsitem.headline: Yawns, derision greet new S.Korean labour law.

text.p: A new labour law that once promised to hone South Korea's industrial competitiveness and herald a financial "big bang" was greeted with yawns and derision on Tuesday.

Share prices slumped, although investors generally ignored the legislation, which was severely watered down after sparking almost four weeks of strikes when it was first rammed through parliament last December.

The new version adopted on Monday delays for two years a key clause designed to smooth financial sector restructuring and help troubled firms stay afloat by making layoffs easier. Layoffs are now all but impossible.
"It's a half-hearted attempt at reform," said Hank Morris, managing director of Coryo Securities.
Kim Sung-shik, senior economist at LG Economic Research Institute, said the legislation was "full of ambiguous clauses and postponements".
"It leaves a bitter feeling that it was rushed through by political parties wanting to get the pressure off their hands in an election year," Kim said.
The law railroaded through parliament in December specifically allowed layoffs in the event of mergers and acquisitions. The new law allows sackings in 1999 on grounds of "management emergency" only.
Analysts said this would stall reform of the over-staffed and inefficient banking sector. Mergers and acquisitions have been touted as the best way to streamline the industry.
Financial reform was given urgency by a scandal this year involving loans to bankrupt Hanbo Steel Co.

"When one looks at the Hanbo scandal -- the quality of credit control, on top of huge inefficiencies -- there's not going to be any help from the labour law in the short term," said Jonathan Dutton, senior analyst at SBC Warburg Securities.
"There had been the spectre of significant layoffs in the banking sector."
President Kim Young-sam agreed to revise the law after strikes cost $3.28 billion in lost output. He had argued that a flexible labour market would boost economic competitiveness.
Kim is barred from seeking a second term in elections in December, but needs public support while he seeks to act as kingmaker and choose a successor.
Richard Samuelson, head of research at SBC Warburg, said the new law did little for efficiency.
"There is no benefit to having a merger. Logic prevailing behind consolidating the banking sector is to fire people and consolidate branches and lower fixed costs."
The Federation of Korean Industries, which represents leading industrial conglomerates, said it would support the new law despite its drawbacks.
"The new law could damage the spirit of financial reform and slow mergers and acquisitions," federation executive Sohn Byung-doo told reporters.
The militant Korean Confederation of Trade Unions, which spearheaded this year's strikes, repeated a threat to organise more industrial stoppages.
"We will fight the law and could strike again until our demands are met," said confederation spokesman Chung Sung-hee.
The stock market's leading index closed down 11.40 points, or 1.7 percent, to 655.95.

"I don't think the labour law will have a major impact on the market because it is very watered down," said Steven Lee, an analyst at Shinyoung Securities. He added: "No one believes unions have enough fighting power left."
